reference.source: ICHD-3 / International Classification of Sleep Disorders
clinicalPearls: Pain is confined to a small, sharply demarcated rounded or elliptical area of the scalp, typically a few centimetres across
The painful patch stays fixed in shape, size and location over time
The parietal region is the most common site, though any part of the scalp may be affected
Local sensory changes such as tenderness, tingling, numbness or allodynia are often present within the zone
Pain may be continuous or intermittent and ranges from mild to moderate
It is thought to arise from terminal branches of the scalp sensory nerves rather than from an intracranial source
Examination and, when indicated, imaging should exclude a local structural or dermatological lesion
reference.pathophysiology: Nummular headache is thought to be a disorder of the terminal twigs of the scalp sensory nerves, producing pain and sensory disturbance restricted to a small, well-defined territory of the epicranial tissues. The sharply localised, fixed area of tenderness and dysaesthesia points to a peripheral, extracranial focus rather than referred or intracranial pain, although central sensitisation may contribute to its persistence.
additionalDifferentials: Local scalp or skull pathology such as a cyst or osteoma
Herpes zoster or post-herpetic neuralgia of the scalp
Giant cell arteritis when the temporal region of an older patient is involved
Referred pain from cervical or dental structures
additionalInvestigations: Careful mapping of the painful area and its associated sensory changes
Palpation for local masses and scalp or skull abnormalities
Skin examination to exclude a dermatological or zoster lesion
Neuroimaging or skull imaging when a structural cause is suspected
Inflammatory markers if giant cell arteritis is a consideration in an older patient
redFlags: A palpable mass, skin change or bony abnormality beneath the painful area
Progressive enlargement of the affected zone
Features of giant cell arteritis in an older patient with temporal involvement
Systemic symptoms or a rapid change in the pain pattern
reference.prognosis: The condition is usually benign; many patients have a chronic but stable course, and symptoms often respond to simple analgesia, gabapentinoids or local injection therapy when troublesome.
pitfalls: Assuming all fixed scalp pain is primary and missing an underlying local lesion
Overlooking giant cell arteritis when the patch overlies the temporal artery in an older patient
Not examining the skin and skull beneath the painful zone
Escalating systemic analgesics without considering targeted local treatment
references: International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition (ICHD-3)
management: Reassurance and simple analgesia for mild, intermittent symptoms
Neuropathic agents such as gabapentinoids or tricyclic antidepressants for troublesome or persistent pain
Local infiltration with anaesthetic and corticosteroid, or botulinum toxin, into the affected scalp zone in refractory cases
Topical agents such as capsaicin or local anaesthetic as an adjunct over the fixed painful patch
Exclusion of a structural scalp or skull lesion, and of giant cell arteritis in older patients, before attributing symptoms to the primary disorder
